name: Shinto
areas: the rites of the farming villages of the Yayoi period
routes: Shrines built under colonial rule in Taiwan (1895–1945)
marks: Shinto has no founder and its roots are prehistoric; Mount Miwa, worshipped as a kami itself, is among its oldest places of worship.
Ritual offerings to the kami were made on this sacred island from the 4th century.
The Grand Shrine of Ise, the shrine of the sun goddess Amaterasu, first rebuilt in 690 and rebuilt every twenty years since.
The Grand Shrine of Izumo, honouring Ōkuninushi, whose myths fill much of the Kojiki (712).
The Kojiki (712), compiled at the court in Nara, records the myths of the kami and the descent of the emperors from the sun goddess.
The Engishiki (927), compiled at the court in Kyoto, lists 2,861 shrines and the court's rituals and prayers.
The shrine later named Yasukuni was founded here in 1869 for those who died fighting for the emperor.
Chōsen Jingū, the chief shrine of colonial Korea (1925), was taken down after Japan's defeat in 1945.
notes: Rice farming spreads through Japan in the Yayoi period; the bronze bells and mirrors of its rituals are among the roots of later kami worship.
The rulers of Yamato build great tomb mounds; ritual offerings to the kami begin on the sacred island of Okinoshima.
Buddhism arrives from Korea (538 or 552), and the worship of the kami begins to be named in contrast to it.
The court organises the worship of the kami around the emperor: the Grand Shrine of Ise is first rebuilt in 690.
The Kojiki (712) and the Nihon Shoki (720) record the myths of the kami and the descent of the emperors from the sun goddess Amaterasu.
Kami and buddhas are worshipped together, and the kami come to be seen as local forms of the buddhas.
The Engishiki (927) lists 2,861 shrines and the court's rituals and prayers.
Storms that wreck the Mongol fleets (1274, 1281) are hailed as "divine winds" (kamikaze).
Yoshida Kanetomo teaches a Shinto independent of Buddhism (Yoshida Shinto).
Scholars of "National Learning" such as Motoori Norinaga (1730–1801) study the Kojiki to recover an ancient Japanese way.
The Meiji government separates kami and buddhas (1868) and builds a State Shinto around the emperor; the shrine later named Yasukuni is founded (1869).
The Allied occupation's Shinto Directive ends State Shinto (1945); shrines become religious corporations.
Most Japanese take part in its festivals and rites at some 80,000 shrines, though few call Shinto their religion.
src: John Breen and Mark Teeuwen, A New History of Shinto (2010)
Inoue Nobutaka (ed.), Shinto: A Short History (2003)
